scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): backs parental involvement while arguing that compulsory volunteering is unfair; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: A school clearly works better when parents take an active part in their children's education.
Some people recommend that all parents should be required to volunteer time at their children's schools.
I agree that parental involvement is valuable, but I believe forcing every parent to volunteer would be unfair and unworkable.
First, parental involvement genuinely benefits children and schools alike.
When parents help out, children often feel more supported and take their schooling more seriously.
For example, a class with parent helpers can give pupils more attention than a single teacher could alone.
This shows that willing parents can make a real and positive difference at school.
Involved parents also understand their children's education better and can support it at home.
Schools with strong parental support often build a warmer and stronger sense of community.
To this extent, encouraging parents to help is plainly a good idea.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why compulsory volunteering is unfair

sentences.text: Second, however, requiring every parent to volunteer would be both unfair and impractical.
Many parents work long hours or hold several jobs and simply cannot spare the time.
Consider a single mother with two jobs who would be punished for failing to give time she cannot afford.
Such a rule would fall hardest on the poorest families, who already struggle the most.
Forced volunteers, moreover, may help unwillingly and add little of real value.
Genuine help comes from willing parents, not from those compelled against their circumstances.
Involvement, then, should be encouraged warmly rather than demanded by force.
In conclusion, parents who help at their children's schools bring real and lasting benefits.
But requiring all parents to volunteer would unfairly burden those who can least afford it.
The wiser path is to welcome and encourage parental help without forcing it on everyone.
